Hindcast CLI — the simulation engine without the UI. (In a checkout of the repository, use "npm run sim --" in place of "hindcast".)

No system handy? A recorded one is built in (no network, no files):
  hindcast demo            [--workspace ./hindcast-demo] [--json]   (the review, a backtest and the accuracy record; --workspace writes the data out)

Start here, on a running system (read-only; one command → a capacity review):
  hindcast quickstart      --prometheus http://prom:9090 [--jaeger http://jaeger:16686 | --tempo http://tempo:3200] [--last 24h]

  hindcast validate        <arch.yaml>
  hindcast simulate        <arch.yaml> [scenario.yaml] [--rps 800 | --traffic metrics.csv] [--duration 60] [--engine fluid|des] [--seed 1] [--json]
                           [--engine des --trace <component> [--failed] [--count 3]]   (sampled requests through it, hop by hop)
  hindcast analyze         <arch.yaml> [scenario.yaml] [--runs 20]       (discrete-event Monte Carlo, 95% CIs)
  hindcast optimize        <arch.yaml> [scenario.yaml] [--runtimes] [--out optimized.yaml]
  hindcast compare         <arch.yaml> <variants.yaml> [scenario.yaml] [--json]
  hindcast breaking-point  <arch.yaml> [--p99 300] [--errors 0.01]
  hindcast audit           <arch.yaml> [--rps 500] [--cost-per-min 1000] [--md report.md] [--html report.html]   (what breaks first, and what it costs)
  hindcast link            <arch.yaml> [variants.yaml]     → open in the app
  hindcast mermaid         <arch.yaml> [--out diagram.mmd]  → a Mermaid flowchart for docs and pull requests
  hindcast import-terraform <terraform-show.json> [--name "My system"] [--out arch.yaml]
  hindcast import-k8s      <manifests.yaml …> [--name "My system"] [--out arch.yaml]      (Deployments, HPAs, StatefulSets, Services, Ingress)
  hindcast catalog
  hindcast mcp            [--http [--port 8787] [--host 127.0.0.1] [--all-tools] [--no-auth]]   (MCP server: stdio, or Streamable HTTP)

Backtesting on real data (files only; see docs/backtest.md):
  hindcast export-prometheus --url http://prom:9090 --start 2026-09-01 --end 2026-09-15 [--step 60] [--preset otel-spanmetrics,cadvisor] --out telemetry/
  hindcast import        <hindcast.import.yaml> [--out dataset.json]
  hindcast calibrate     <dataset.json> [--out model.json] [--p99 500] [--errors 0.01] [--timeout 5000] [--holdout 0.3]
  hindcast backtest      <model.json> <dataset.json> <strategy.yaml …> [--last 14d] [--scale 2 | --peak 400] [--draws 30] [--md r.md] [--html r.html] [--comment pr.md] [--card card.json] [--gate]
  hindcast headroom      <model.json> [strategy.yaml]
  hindcast accuracy      <model.json>
  hindcast outage        <model.json> <outage-id | list> [strategy.yaml …] [--role primary-db=orders-db] [--md r.md] [--html r.html]
  hindcast diff-strategy --base <dir> --head <dir> [--model model.json] [--out strategy.yaml]   (k8s manifests before/after → strategy)
  hindcast verify-change --model model.json --dataset dataset.json (--base <dir> --head <dir> | --terraform-plan plan.json | <strategy.yaml …>)
                         [--last 14d] [--p99 500] [--errors 0.01] [--comment pr.md] [--json result.json] [--fail-on fail|inconclusive|never]   (the verify_change verdict, for CI)
  hindcast loadtest plan  [strategy.yaml …] [--base <dir> --head <dir>] [--service frontend[=0.9],…] [--workspace .hindcast] [--scale 1.3] [--out loadtest.k6.js] [--json]
                         (the load test a low-confidence verdict asks for: targets, a step-load k6 script, the follow-up)

For agents (the MCP tools, from a shell; JSON in, JSON out; see docs/agents.md):
  hindcast agent setup [claude|cursor|vscode|desktop|windsurf] [--write]   register the MCP server with an agent host
  hindcast agent list
  hindcast agent <tool> '<json args>' | @args.json | -      e.g. agent connect_telemetry '{"prometheus":{"url":"http://prom:9090"}}'
  tools: connect_telemetry collect_telemetry calibrate_model model_status review_capacity suggest_changes verify_change
         plan_load_test check_node_loss find_headroom verify_design read_cluster

Files may be YAML or JSON. A variants file is either a list of variants or { variants, scenario }.

# Backtest — HotROD

Replayed **0.7 hours** of real traffic (2026-10-07T16:20 → 2026-10-07T17:01 UTC, 30s buckets) through the calibrated model, 6 draws per strategy (replays with each service's capacity drawn from its fitted range). Ranges are 10th–90th percentiles: 8 in 10 draws fall inside.

SLO: p99 ≤ 1000 ms and errors ≤ 3.0%.

## Ranking

| # | strategy | $/month vs as built | minutes out of SLO | failed requests | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| – | As built | $95.56/month | 14 min (14 min … 15 min) | 1,616 (932 … 2,018) | |
| 1 | Autoscale customer on CPU | ±$0.00 | 14 min (14 min … 15 min) | 1,616 (932 … 2,018) | costs the same, with no change in time out of SLO |

## As built

the calibrated model with nothing changed

- cost over the window $0.09 · $95.56/month
- 14 min (14 min … 15 min) out of SLO, 1,616 (932 … 2,018) failed requests, 462% of the error budget
- worst moment: Oct 7 at 16:51 UTC — p99 5000 ms, 100.0% errors; mysql at 84% of capacity (7.5 req/s on 1 × 8.9 req/s), still draining a 18.0 s backlog

| from | minutes | peak p99 | peak errors | why |

| Oct 7 at 16:34 UTC | 0.5 | 804 ms | 3.1% | mysql at 71% of capacity (6.3 req/s on 1 × 8.9 req/s), 174 ms wait |

# Capacity review — my system

History 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53 UTC, busiest moment 35.8 req/s (requests a second). SLO, the target: p99 ≤ 500 ms (99% of requests answered within it), errors ≤ 1.0%; time out of SLO is the minutes that missed it.

## Summary

- **Risk:** **Medium.** The recorded day held, but a 2× day spends 13.5 min out of SLO — api at 97% of capacity (71.6 req/s on 1 × 73.8 req/s), 352 ms wait. And losing **node-a** at the busiest moment fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO.
- **Headroom:** 67.8 req/s within SLO, 1.89× the busiest moment (35.8 req/s); api saturates first. Its limit is read from CPU alone: api has no latency metric.
- **Headroom uncertain:** 27.3–67.8 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone).
- **Cost:** about **$280/month** as run ($3,360 a year), on 2 nodes 31% full at the busiest moment; a commitment on the always-on floor saves up to $152/month.
- **Do this:** run api × 2, worker × 2 spread over the nodes, so losing one leaves a replica of each — no added cost (it fits on the nodes already running). Run `verify_change` on it before it ships.
- **Trust:** 1 of 1 services fit the history well. No traces: no calls named in the metrics — api, worker read against the entry traffic; no per-endpoint latency; no latency metric for api, worker (capacity from CPU, throttling and memory). On history it was not fitted to, its latency predictions (p99) were off by 2% (inside the 20% tolerance).

## Headroom

Within SLO up to **67.8 req/s** — 1.89× the busiest moment; api saturates first.

**Uncertain:** 27.3–67.8 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone). Each third of the history's traffic, calibrated alone: 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 18:53: 27.3 req/s, web first; 8 Oct 2026 18:53 – 8 Oct 2026 20:53: 36.4 req/s, web first; 8 Oct 2026 20:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53: 65.7 req/s, web first.

- **The recorded day, replayed:** holds
- **1.5× today's traffic:** holds
- **2× today's traffic:** 13.5 min out of SLO, 1,080 failed requests — api at 97% of capacity (71.6 req/s on 1 × 73.8 req/s), 352 ms wait

## Losing a node at the busiest moment

Losing **node-a** fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO: api has no replica left.

Single points of failure (every replica on one node): api, worker.

Fix, backtested: api → 2, worker → 2, spread over the nodes — survives every node, +$0/month.

## Limits that bind

- **api** peaked at 203 MiB of its 256 MiB memory limit (79%)

## Node pool

2 nodes of 4 cores and 16 GiB, a fixed pool. At the busiest moment every pod's requests fill **31%** of it.

It can't shrink: 2 nodes is the fewest that hold the busiest moment's requests with one node to spare for losing one.

## Commitment

The history never ran fewer than **2 nodes** ($280/month on demand): capacity that is always on, which a commitment discounts. 1-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$93/month**; 3-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$152/month**.

Nodes priced as EC2 m6i on demand; reserved m6i is 33% / 54% off (no upfront). Commit to the floor, not the peak: what runs above it stays on demand.

Every number is a replay of the recorded history through the calibrated model; `verify_change` the one you ship for its full evidence.

# Capacity review — my system

History 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53 UTC, busiest moment 35.8 req/s (requests a second). SLO, the target: p99 ≤ 500 ms (99% of requests answered within it), errors ≤ 1.0%; time out of SLO is the minutes that missed it.

## Summary

- **Risk:** **Medium.** Traffic holds to 2×, but losing **node-a** at the busiest moment fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO.
- **Headroom:** 115.6 req/s within SLO, 3.23× the busiest moment (35.8 req/s); cart saturates first.
- **Headroom uncertain:** 25.8–115.6 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone).
- **Cost:** about **$280/month** as run ($3,360 a year), on 2 nodes 31% full at the busiest moment; a commitment on the always-on floor saves up to $152/month.
- **Do this:** run cart × 2, catalog × 2, flagd × 2, valkey-cart × 2 spread over the nodes, so losing one leaves a replica of each — no added cost (it fits on the nodes already running). Run `verify_change` on it before it ships.
- **Also check:** a restart of flagd or catalog may leave callers' gRPC channels broken; check keepalive/reconnect settings — the replay times only the platform's recovery.
- **Trust:** 3 of 3 services fit the history well. No traces: topology from span metrics (client spans matched to the servers that answer them); no per-endpoint latency; no latency metric for flagd, valkey-cart (capacity from CPU, throttling and memory). On history it was not fitted to, its latency predictions (p99) were off by 4% (inside the 20% tolerance).

## Headroom

Within SLO up to **115.6 req/s** — 3.23× the busiest moment; cart saturates first.

**Uncertain:** 25.8–115.6 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone). Each third of the history's traffic, calibrated alone: 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 18:53: 25.8 req/s, catalog first; 8 Oct 2026 18:53 – 8 Oct 2026 20:53: 35.3 req/s, frontend first; 8 Oct 2026 20:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53: 53.1 req/s, frontend first.

- **The recorded day, replayed:** holds
- **1.5× today's traffic:** holds
- **2× today's traffic:** holds

## Losing a node at the busiest moment

Losing **node-a** fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO: cart has no replica left.

Single points of failure (every replica on one node): cart, catalog, flagd, valkey-cart.

Fix, backtested: cart → 2, catalog → 2, flagd → 2, valkey-cart → 2, spread over the nodes — survives every node, +$0/month.

## Risks the replay doesn't time

A restart of any of these single-replica services may leave callers' gRPC channels broken; check keepalive/reconnect settings — the replay times only the platform's recovery:

- **flagd**, called over gRPC by cart
- **catalog**, called over gRPC by frontend

## Node pool

2 nodes of 4 cores and 16 GiB, a fixed pool. At the busiest moment every pod's requests fill **31%** of it.

It can't shrink: 2 nodes is the fewest that hold the busiest moment's requests with one node to spare for losing one.

## Commitment

The history never ran fewer than **2 nodes** ($280/month on demand): capacity that is always on, which a commitment discounts. 1-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$93/month**; 3-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$152/month**.

Nodes priced as EC2 m6i on demand; reserved m6i is 33% / 54% off (no upfront). Commit to the floor, not the peak: what runs above it stays on demand.

Every number is a replay of the recorded history through the calibrated model; `verify_change` the one you ship for its full evidence.

# Capacity review — my system

History 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53 UTC, busiest moment 71.6 req/s (requests a second). SLO, the target: p99 ≤ 500 ms (99% of requests answered within it), errors ≤ 1.0%; time out of SLO is the minutes that missed it.

## Summary

- **Risk:** **Medium.** The recorded day held, but a 1.5× day spends 9.8 min out of SLO — no component near its limit (busiest: cart at 43%). And losing **node-a** at the busiest moment fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO.
- **Headroom:** 248.7 req/s within SLO, 3.48× the busiest moment (71.6 req/s); cart saturates first. That is on the history's average mix of requests; replayed moment by moment, a 1.5× day already goes out of SLO, so read the real headroom as under 1.5×.
- **Headroom uncertain:** 52.8–248.7 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone).
- **Cost:** about **$280/month** as run ($3,360 a year), on 2 nodes 31% full at the busiest moment; a commitment on the always-on floor saves up to $152/month.
- **Do this:** run cart × 2, catalog × 2 spread over the nodes, so losing one leaves a replica of each — no added cost (it fits on the nodes already running). Run `verify_change` on it before it ships.
- **Also check:** a restart of catalog may leave callers' gRPC channels broken; check keepalive/reconnect settings — the replay times only the platform's recovery.
- **Trust:** 3 of 3 services fit the history well. No traces: topology from span metrics (client spans matched to the servers that answer them); no per-endpoint latency. On history it was not fitted to, its latency predictions (p99) were off by 41% (outside the 20% tolerance: read every number as directional).

## Headroom

Within SLO up to **248.7 req/s** — 3.48× the busiest moment; cart saturates first.

That is on the history's average mix of requests; replayed moment by moment, a 1.5× day already goes out of SLO, so read the real headroom as under 1.5×.

**Uncertain:** 52.8–248.7 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone). Each third of the history's traffic, calibrated alone: 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 18:53: 52.8 req/s, catalog first; 8 Oct 2026 18:53 – 8 Oct 2026 20:53: 74.6 req/s, frontend first; 8 Oct 2026 20:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53: 108.1 req/s, cart first.

- **The recorded day, replayed:** holds
- **1.5× today's traffic:** 9.8 min out of SLO, 1,619 failed requests — no component near its limit (busiest: cart at 43%)
- **2× today's traffic:** 70.5 min out of SLO, 2,159 failed requests — cart at 58% of capacity (71.6 req/s on 1 × 123.8 req/s), 9 ms wait

## Losing a node at the busiest moment

Losing **node-a** fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO: cart has no replica left.

Single points of failure (every replica on one node): cart, catalog, valkey-cart, flagd.

Fix, backtested: cart → 2, catalog → 2, spread over the nodes — survives every node, +$0/month.

## Risks the replay doesn't time

A restart of catalog may leave callers' gRPC channels broken; check keepalive/reconnect settings — the replay times only the platform's recovery. catalog runs one replica; frontend calls it over gRPC.

## Node pool

2 nodes of 4 cores and 16 GiB, a fixed pool. At the busiest moment every pod's requests fill **31%** of it.

It can't shrink: 2 nodes is the fewest that hold the busiest moment's requests with one node to spare for losing one.

## Commitment

The history never ran fewer than **2 nodes** ($280/month on demand): capacity that is always on, which a commitment discounts. 1-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$93/month**; 3-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$152/month**.

Nodes priced as EC2 m6i on demand; reserved m6i is 33% / 54% off (no upfront). Commit to the floor, not the peak: what runs above it stays on demand.

Every number is a replay of the recorded history through the calibrated model; `verify_change` the one you ship for its full evidence.

# Capacity review — my system

History 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53 UTC, busiest moment 35.8 req/s (requests a second). SLO, the target: p99 ≤ 500 ms (99% of requests answered within it), errors ≤ 1.0%; time out of SLO is the minutes that missed it.

## Summary

- **Risk:** **Medium.** Traffic holds to 2×, but losing **node-a** at the busiest moment fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO.
- **Headroom:** 115.6 req/s within SLO, 3.23× the busiest moment (35.8 req/s); cart saturates first.
- **Headroom uncertain:** 25.8–115.6 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone).
- **Cost:** about **$280/month** as run ($3,360 a year), on 2 nodes 31% full at the busiest moment; a commitment on the always-on floor saves up to $152/month.
- **Do this:** run cart × 2, catalog × 2 spread over the nodes, so losing one leaves a replica of each — no added cost (it fits on the nodes already running). Run `verify_change` on it before it ships.
- **Also check:** a restart of catalog may leave callers' gRPC channels broken; check keepalive/reconnect settings — the replay times only the platform's recovery.
- **Trust:** 3 of 3 services fit the history well. No traces: topology from the OpenTelemetry service graph; no per-endpoint latency. On history it was not fitted to, its latency predictions (p99) were off by 4% (inside the 20% tolerance).

## Headroom

Within SLO up to **115.6 req/s** — 3.23× the busiest moment; cart saturates first.

**Uncertain:** 25.8–115.6 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone). Each third of the history's traffic, calibrated alone: 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 18:53: 25.8 req/s, catalog first; 8 Oct 2026 18:53 – 8 Oct 2026 20:53: 35.3 req/s, frontend first; 8 Oct 2026 20:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53: 53.1 req/s, frontend first.

- **The recorded day, replayed:** holds
- **1.5× today's traffic:** holds
- **2× today's traffic:** holds

## Losing a node at the busiest moment

Losing **node-a** fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO: cart has no replica left.

Single points of failure (every replica on one node): cart, catalog, valkey-cart, flagd.

Fix, backtested: cart → 2, catalog → 2, spread over the nodes — survives every node, +$0/month.

## Risks the replay doesn't time

A restart of catalog may leave callers' gRPC channels broken; check keepalive/reconnect settings — the replay times only the platform's recovery. catalog runs one replica; frontend calls it over gRPC.

## Node pool

2 nodes of 4 cores and 16 GiB, a fixed pool. At the busiest moment every pod's requests fill **31%** of it.

It can't shrink: 2 nodes is the fewest that hold the busiest moment's requests with one node to spare for losing one.

## Commitment

The history never ran fewer than **2 nodes** ($280/month on demand): capacity that is always on, which a commitment discounts. 1-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$93/month**; 3-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$152/month**.

Nodes priced as EC2 m6i on demand; reserved m6i is 33% / 54% off (no upfront). Commit to the floor, not the peak: what runs above it stays on demand.

Every number is a replay of the recorded history through the calibrated model; `verify_change` the one you ship for its full evidence.

# Capacity review — my system

History 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53 UTC, busiest moment 35.8 req/s (requests a second). SLO, the target: p99 ≤ 500 ms (99% of requests answered within it), errors ≤ 1.0%; time out of SLO is the minutes that missed it.

## Summary

- **Risk:** **Medium.** Traffic holds to 2×, but losing **node-a** at the busiest moment fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO.
- **Headroom:** 115.6 req/s within SLO, 3.23× the busiest moment (35.8 req/s); cart saturates first.
- **Headroom uncertain:** 25.8–115.6 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone).
- **Cost:** about **$280/month** as run ($3,360 a year), on 2 nodes 31% full at the busiest moment; a commitment on the always-on floor saves up to $152/month.
- **Do this:** run cart × 2, catalog × 2, flagd × 2, valkey-cart × 2 spread over the nodes, so losing one leaves a replica of each — no added cost (it fits on the nodes already running). Run `verify_change` on it before it ships.
- **Also check:** a restart of flagd or catalog may leave callers' gRPC channels broken; check keepalive/reconnect settings — the replay times only the platform's recovery.
- **Trust:** 3 of 3 services fit the history well. No traces: topology from span metrics (client spans matched to the servers that answer them); no per-endpoint latency; no latency metric for flagd, valkey-cart (capacity from CPU, throttling and memory). On history it was not fitted to, its latency predictions (p99) were off by 4% (inside the 20% tolerance).

## Headroom

Within SLO up to **115.6 req/s** — 3.23× the busiest moment; cart saturates first.

**Uncertain:** 25.8–115.6 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone). Each third of the history's traffic, calibrated alone: 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 18:53: 25.8 req/s, catalog first; 8 Oct 2026 18:53 – 8 Oct 2026 20:53: 35.3 req/s, frontend first; 8 Oct 2026 20:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53: 53.1 req/s, frontend first.

- **The recorded day, replayed:** holds
- **1.5× today's traffic:** holds
- **2× today's traffic:** holds

## Losing a node at the busiest moment

Losing **node-a** fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO: cart has no replica left.

Single points of failure (every replica on one node): cart, catalog, flagd, valkey-cart.

Fix, backtested: cart → 2, catalog → 2, flagd → 2, valkey-cart → 2, spread over the nodes — survives every node, +$0/month.

## Risks the replay doesn't time

A restart of any of these single-replica services may leave callers' gRPC channels broken; check keepalive/reconnect settings — the replay times only the platform's recovery:

- **flagd**, called over gRPC by cart
- **catalog**, called over gRPC by frontend

## Node pool

2 nodes of 4 cores and 16 GiB, a fixed pool. At the busiest moment every pod's requests fill **31%** of it.

It can't shrink: 2 nodes is the fewest that hold the busiest moment's requests with one node to spare for losing one.

## Commitment

The history never ran fewer than **2 nodes** ($280/month on demand): capacity that is always on, which a commitment discounts. 1-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$93/month**; 3-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$152/month**.

Nodes priced as EC2 m6i on demand; reserved m6i is 33% / 54% off (no upfront). Commit to the floor, not the peak: what runs above it stays on demand.

Every number is a replay of the recorded history through the calibrated model; `verify_change` the one you ship for its full evidence.

# Capacity review — my system

History 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53 UTC, busiest moment 35.8 req/s (requests a second). SLO, the target: p99 ≤ 500 ms (99% of requests answered within it), errors ≤ 1.0%; time out of SLO is the minutes that missed it.

## Summary

- **Risk:** **Medium.** The recorded day held, but a 2× day spends 13.5 min out of SLO — api at 97% of capacity (71.6 req/s on 1 × 73.8 req/s), 352 ms wait. And losing **node-a** at the busiest moment fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO.
- **Headroom:** 67.8 req/s within SLO, 1.89× the busiest moment (35.8 req/s); api saturates first. Its limit is read from CPU alone: api has no latency metric.
- **Headroom uncertain:** 27.3–67.8 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone).
- **Cost:** about **$280/month** as run ($3,360 a year), on 2 nodes 31% full at the busiest moment; a commitment on the always-on floor saves up to $152/month.
- **Do this:** run api × 2, worker × 2, jaeger × 2 spread over the nodes, so losing one leaves a replica of each — no added cost (it fits on the nodes already running). Run `verify_change` on it before it ships.
- **Trust:** 1 of 1 services fit the history well. No traces: no calls named in the metrics — api, worker, jaeger read against the entry traffic; no per-endpoint latency; no latency metric for api, worker, jaeger (capacity from CPU, throttling and memory). On history it was not fitted to, its latency predictions (p99) were off by 2% (inside the 20% tolerance).

## Headroom

Within SLO up to **67.8 req/s** — 1.89× the busiest moment; api saturates first.

**Uncertain:** 27.3–67.8 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone). Each third of the history's traffic, calibrated alone: 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 18:53: 27.3 req/s, web first; 8 Oct 2026 18:53 – 8 Oct 2026 20:53: 36.4 req/s, web first; 8 Oct 2026 20:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:53: 65.7 req/s, web first.

- **The recorded day, replayed:** holds
- **1.5× today's traffic:** holds
- **2× today's traffic:** 13.5 min out of SLO, 1,080 failed requests — api at 97% of capacity (71.6 req/s on 1 × 73.8 req/s), 352 ms wait

## Losing a node at the busiest moment

Losing **node-a** fails 5,242 more requests and 2.5 min out of SLO: api has no replica left.

Single points of failure (every replica on one node): api, worker, jaeger.

Fix, backtested: api → 2, worker → 2, jaeger → 2, spread over the nodes — survives every node, +$0/month.

## Limits that bind

- **api** peaked at 203 MiB of its 256 MiB memory limit (79%)

## Node pool

2 nodes of 4 cores and 16 GiB, a fixed pool. At the busiest moment every pod's requests fill **31%** of it.

It can't shrink: 2 nodes is the fewest that hold the busiest moment's requests with one node to spare for losing one.

## Commitment

The history never ran fewer than **2 nodes** ($280/month on demand): capacity that is always on, which a commitment discounts. 1-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$93/month**; 3-year reserved (no upfront) saves about **$152/month**.

Nodes priced as EC2 m6i on demand; reserved m6i is 33% / 54% off (no upfront). Commit to the floor, not the peak: what runs above it stays on demand.

Every number is a replay of the recorded history through the calibrated model; `verify_change` the one you ship for its full evidence.

# Backtest — Astronomy Shop

Replayed **5.5 hours** of real traffic (2021-01-04T13:30 → 2021-01-04T19:00 UTC, 60s buckets) through the calibrated model, 10 draws per strategy (replays with each service's capacity drawn from its fitted range). Ranges are 10th–90th percentiles: 8 in 10 draws fall inside.

SLO: p99 ≤ 800 ms and errors ≤ 1.0%.

## Ranking

| # | strategy | $/month vs as built | minutes out of SLO | failed requests | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| – | As built | $230/month | 260 min | 188,321 (188,280 … 188,383) | |
| 1 | Autoscale the frontend | +$25.65 | 260 min | 188,280 | costs $26/month more, with no change in time out of SLO |

## As built

the calibrated model with nothing changed

- cost over the window $1.73 · $230/month
- 260 min out of SLO, 188,321 (188,280 … 188,383) failed requests, 508% of the error budget
- worst moment: Jan 4 at 15:00 UTC — p99 4524 ms, 6.4% errors; frontend at 93% of capacity (259.4 req/s on 1 × 277.8 req/s), 51 ms wait

| from | minutes | peak p99 | peak errors | why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 4 at 14:20 UTC | 260.0 | 4524 ms | 6.4% | frontend at 93% of capacity (259.4 req/s on 1 × 277.8 req/s), 51 ms wait |

## Autoscale the frontend

Target-tracking on CPU, 1–4 replicas behind the load balancer — instead of sizing for the peak.

- frontend: autoscale 1–4 replicas at 60% CPU, 10 s warm-up, 120 s cool-down

- cost over the window $1.93 · $256/month
- 260 min out of SLO, 188,280 failed requests, 508% of the error budget
- worst moment: Jan 4 at 15:00 UTC — p99 4361 ms, 6.4% errors; no component near its limit (busiest: recommendation at 42%)

| from | minutes | peak p99 | peak errors | why |

| Jan 4 at 14:20 UTC | 260.0 | 4361 ms | 6.4% | no component near its limit (busiest: recommendation at 42%) |

# Failure audit — Web shop

At **1,500 req/s** (80% reads), SLO: errors ≤ 1.0%, p99 ≤ 300 ms.

| | |
|---|---|
| Resilience score | **0/100** — survives 0 of 8 incidents within SLO |
| Availability, SLA (published), not measured | 99.5% — about 44.7 h of downtime a year; costs the most: db (43.8 h), lb (54 min) |
| Headroom | 0.7× — 1,000 req/s, then **api** gives out |
| Normal operation | errors 33.3%, p99 incl. failures 1.1 s, $971/month — **already outside the SLO** |

## What breaks first

| severity | incident | users see | recovers | blast radius | best verified fix | $/month |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Critical | traffic surges 3× for 20 s | 33.6% errors, peak p99 incl. failures 1.1 s | **never** (metastable) | — | Scale api to 8 instances → major | $292 |
| Critical | db goes down | 63.2% errors, peak p99 incl. failures 1.1 s | **never** (metastable) | api | Add a read replica to db → critical | $562 |
| Critical | lb goes down | 64.2% errors, peak p99 incl. failures 1.1 s | **never** (metastable) | api | Run a standby lb → critical | $36 |
| Critical | db turns slow (+250 ms) | 57.0% errors, peak p99 incl. failures 2.4 s | **never** (metastable) | api | Timeout + circuit breaker with fallback on api → db → critical | $0 |
| Critical | one api instance dies | 16.2% errors, peak p99 incl. failures 1.1 s | **never** (metastable) | — | Run 5 × api → critical | $73 |
| Critical | api fails 20% of requests | 12.5% errors, peak p99 incl. failures 1.1 s | **never** (metastable) | — | Retry budget + circuit breaker with fallback on lb → critical | $0 |
| Critical | db fails 20% of requests | 12.4% errors, peak p99 incl. failures 1.1 s | **never** (metastable) | api | 2 retries with backoff on api → critical | $0 |
| Critical | api turns slow (+250 ms) | 0.0% errors, peak p99 incl. failures 1.4 s | **never** (metastable) | — | Timeout + circuit breaker with fallback on lb → api → major | $0 |
| Critical | load ramps past 1000 req/s | 0.0% errors, peak p99 incl. failures 0 ms | — | api | Scale api to 8 instances → major | $292 |

## All incidents

### Critical: traffic surges 3× for 20 s

33.6% of requests failed while it lasted (peak 77.8%), p99 incl. failures up to 1.1 s. Did not recover after the fault was cleared — a metastable failure: the system stays overloaded by its own retries or backlog.

**$962 at risk** per incident.

Verified fixes (re-ran the same incident):

- **Scale api to 8 instances** — Double the fleet. After: major, 5.7% errors. $292/month. `api: instances = 8`
- **Size api up to M** — Bigger instance class: about twice the throughput. After: major, 5.7% errors. $350/month. `api: tier = M`
- **Autoscale api (4–16, 15 s warm-up)** — Pay for the surge only while it lasts — as long as capacity arrives fast enough. After: major, 14.5% errors. $407/month. `api: autoscale = {"min":4,"max":16,"warmupS":15,"cooldownS":60}`

### Critical: db goes down

63.2% of requests failed while it lasted (peak 100.0%), p99 incl. failures up to 1.1 s. Did not recover after the fault was cleared — a metastable failure: the system stays overloaded by its own retries or backlog. Knock-on: api — Overloaded: 1.5k req/s offered vs 1.0k req/s capacity. The excess queues, then gets dropped.

**$680 at risk** per incident.

Verified fixes (re-ran the same incident):

- **Add a read replica to db** — A replica serves reads, keeps serving them while the primary is down, and is promoted to primary in about a minute (RDS Multi-AZ: 60–120 s); writes fail until then. After: critical, 12.4% errors. $562/month. `add db-replica (replica); connect db → db-replica`

### Critical: lb goes down

64.2% of requests failed while it lasted (peak 100.0%), p99 incl. failures up to 1.1 s. Did not recover after the fault was cleared — a metastable failure: the system stays overloaded by its own retries or backlog. Knock-on: api — Overloaded: 1.5k req/s offered vs 1.0k req/s capacity. The excess queues, then gets dropped.

**$669 at risk** per incident.

Verified fixes (re-ran the same incident):

- **Run a standby lb** — A second load balancer that callers fail over to. After: critical, 0.60% errors. $36/month. `add lb-b (lb); connect users → lb-b; users: routing = failover; connect lb-b → api`

### Critical: db turns slow (+250 ms)

57.0% of requests failed while it lasted (peak 94.9%), p99 incl. failures up to 2.4 s. Did not recover after the fault was cleared — a metastable failure: the system stays overloaded by its own retries or backlog. db spends 250 ms more on each request than its 10 ms of work, so each worker is busy 26× as long: it serves about 77 req/s instead of 2,000, under the 988 req/s it is offered, and sheds the rest. The incident is a gray failure of the component itself; slowness in the network in front of it would be `latencyMs` on the connection. Knock-on: api — Overloaded: 1.5k req/s offered vs 1.0k req/s capacity. The excess queues, then gets dropped.

**$614 at risk** per incident.

Verified fixes (re-ran the same incident):

- **Timeout + circuit breaker with fallback on api → db** — Give up quickly on the slow dependency and serve a degraded answer instead of making every answer wait for it. After: critical, 5.1% errors. $0/month. `api: timeoutMs = 200, breaker = true, fallback = true`

### Critical: one api instance dies

16.2% of requests failed while it lasted (peak 51.4%), p99 incl. failures up to 1.1 s. Did not recover after the fault was cleared — a metastable failure: the system stays overloaded by its own retries or backlog.

**$168 at risk** per incident.

Verified fixes (re-ran the same incident):

- **Run 5 × api** — One more instance than the load needs (N+1): losing one leaves enough capacity. After: critical. $73/month. `api: instances = 5`

### Critical: api fails 20% of requests

12.5% of requests failed while it lasted (peak 46.7%), p99 incl. failures up to 1.1 s. Did not recover after the fault was cleared — a metastable failure: the system stays overloaded by its own retries or backlog.

**$133 at risk** per incident.

Verified fixes (re-ran the same incident):

- **Retry budget + circuit breaker with fallback on lb** — Retry the occasional failure (within a 10 % budget so retries cannot snowball), cut off a dependency that keeps failing. After: critical. $0/month. `lb: retries = 2, retryPolicy = budget, breaker = true, fallback = true`

### Critical: db fails 20% of requests

12.4% of requests failed while it lasted (peak 46.7%), p99 incl. failures up to 1.1 s. Did not recover after the fault was cleared — a metastable failure: the system stays overloaded by its own retries or backlog. Knock-on: api — Overloaded: 1.5k req/s offered vs 1.0k req/s capacity. The excess queues, then gets dropped.

**$133 at risk** per incident.

Verified fixes (re-ran the same incident):

- **2 retries with backoff on api** — Most transient errors succeed on a second try; backoff with jitter spreads the extra load. After: critical, 0.50% errors. $0/month. `api: retries = 2, retryPolicy = backoff`

### Critical: api turns slow (+250 ms)

0.00% of requests failed while it lasted (peak 33.3%), p99 incl. failures up to 1.4 s. Did not recover after the fault was cleared — a metastable failure: the system stays overloaded by its own retries or backlog. api has no thread limit, so slow calls wait without holding a worker: it adds 250 ms to every answer but keeps serving.

Verified fixes (re-ran the same incident):

- **Timeout + circuit breaker with fallback on lb → api** — Give up quickly on the slow dependency and serve a degraded answer instead of making every answer wait for it. After: major. $0/month. `lb: timeoutMs = 200, breaker = true, fallback = true`

### Critical: load ramps past 1000 req/s

Sustains 1000 req/s within SLO — 0.7× the expected 1500 req/s. api gives out first: Saturated at 101% — requests are queuing and latency is climbing steeply.

Verified fixes (re-ran the same incident):

- **Scale api to 8 instances** — Double the fleet. Sustains 2000 req/s (1.3×), then api is next. After: major. $292/month. `api: instances = 8`
- **Size api up to M** — Bigger instance class: about twice the throughput. Sustains 2000 req/s (1.3×), then api is next. After: major. $350/month. `api: tier = M`

# Capacity review — my system

History 8 Oct 2026 16:53 – 8 Oct 2026 22:54 UTC, busiest moment 35.5 req/s (requests a second). SLO, the target: p99 ≤ 500 ms (99% of requests answered within it), errors ≤ 1.0%; time out of SLO is the minutes that missed it.

## Summary

- **Risk:** **Medium.** The recorded day held, but a 1.5× day spends 24.5 min out of SLO — cart at 59% of capacity (32.0 req/s on 1 × 54.2 req/s), 5 ms wait.
- **Headroom:** 52.9 req/s within SLO, 1.49× the busiest moment (35.5 req/s); cart saturates first.
- **Headroom uncertain:** 26.7–52.9 req/s depending on the window (the whole history, and each third of its traffic calibrated alone).
- **Cost:** about **$175/month** as run ($2,100 a year); a commitment on the always-on floor saves up to $35/month; the best saving that passes: postgres on Graviton (−$13/month); all of them together pass too (−$35/month).

files.demo/strategies/1-autoscale-frontend.yam:
name: Autoscale the frontend
description: Target-tracking on CPU, 1–4 replicas behind the load balancer — instead of sizing for the peak.
changes:
  - service: frontend
    autoscale: { min: 1, max: 4, targetCpu: 0.6, warmupS: 10, cooldownS: 120, intervalS: 15 }
files.demo/strategies/2-frontend-1cpu.yaml:
name: Frontend on 1 vCPU
description: Double the frontend's CPU limit (0.5 → 1 core). It is CPU-bound, so capacity should follow.
changes:
  - service: frontend
    cpu: 1
files.demo/strategies/3-graviton.yaml:
name: Frontend and cart on Graviton
description: Arm pricing for the two busiest services; equal throughput assumed until benchmarked.
changes:
  - service: frontend
    arch: arm
  - service: cart
    arch: arm
files.demo/strategies/4-catalog-cache.yaml:
name: Cache in front of the product catalog
description: 80% of catalog lookups served from a cache node (ElastiCache cache.r7g.large).
changes:
  - service: product-catalog
    cache: { hitRate: 0.8 }
